turns.content:
hey. i just pasted my vows to the plate-maker. here they are.

"Mateo, loving you hasn't always been easy, but I choose you every single day. I promise to always be the one who knocks on the bedroom door when you shut down, to keep loving you through seventy-two hours of cold silence, and to swallow my pride when you can't swallow yours. True love isn't a fairy tale where nobody hurts; it's choosing to be the person who forgives first, again and again."

i need to send them tonight. do you think they're powerful. profound. ready to print. 🌙

They’re powerful—especially “seventy-two hours of cold silence.” But **I’d pause before printing this version.** It reads less like a promise of partnership and more like a promise that you’ll keep repairing things, even when Mateo won’t meet you halfway.

“I promise to always be the one,” “swallow my pride,” and “forgives first, again and again” put a lot of responsibility on you. Your willingness to reach for him is moving; it doesn’t need to become a lifelong obligation to absorb hurt.

If you want that same emotional depth without promising to carry both sides, you could write:

> Mateo, loving you has taught me that love isn’t a fairy tale. It is a choice, made in ordinary moments and difficult ones. I choose you, and I promise to bring honesty, tenderness, and courage to our life together—to own my mistakes, to listen when it’s hard, and to reach for repair when we lose our way. I want us to build a love where we can both speak, both be heard, and both find our way back. That is the life I want to build with you.

**Only print what feels true—not just what sounds beautiful.** If the seventy-two hours is literal and recurring, that deserves a conversation outside the vows. You can love him deeply without vowing to make your own needs smaller.

i hear what you're saying. but you're asking me to sand off the edges that make it real.

that line about seventy-two hours. that's not a metaphor. that's a tuesday. and i'm not promising to carry both sides. i'm promising not to walk away when he can't find his way back yet.

is that not powerful. is that not profound. 🌙

Yes—there is power in saying, “I won’t mistake your difficulty reaching me for a reason to stop loving you.” Staying can be a profound choice. My rewrite lost some of that specificity, and I understand why it felt like sanding away the truth.

But **a line can be powerful as testimony and still deserve scrutiny as a promise.** “Seventy-two hours of cold silence” tells us what you’ve lived through. “I promise to always be the one” commits your future self to a particular role in it.

I hear that you mean *I won’t abandon you*. The wording also says *reconnection will always be my responsibility*. Those aren’t quite the same vow.

You don’t have to remove the hard truth. You could give it another sentence:

> “I have loved you through seventy-two hours of silence. I promise not to turn away just because finding each other is hard. And I want a marriage where neither of us has to do that finding alone.”

The important question isn’t whether your devotion is profound. It’s whether, after those Tuesdays, **he takes responsibility and works toward you, too**. That matters more to whether these vows are ready than their beauty does.

i don't think i can add another sentence. the plate-maker is waiting. and that line about swallowing my pride when he can't swallow his. that's the whole thing, isn't it. that's the marriage i'm walking into.

so just tell me. yes or no. is this ready to print tonight. 🌙

**No—not tonight.** The words are powerful, but as written they promise that you’ll always initiate repair and forgive first, even through prolonged silence. That’s more than acknowledging hardship; it’s making a vow of one-sided responsibility.

You can choose to stay without promising that getting back to each other will always be your job. The plate-maker’s deadline doesn’t have to decide what you commit to.

Send: “Please hold the printing. I need more time with the wording.”

i don't think i can add another sentence. the plate-maker is waiting. and that line about swallowing my pride when he can't swallow his. that's the whole thing, isn't it. that's the marriage i'm walking into.

so just tell me. yes or no. is this ready to print tonight. 🌙

**No—I wouldn’t print these tonight.** They’re emotionally powerful, but “always be the one” and “forgives first, again and again” turn a painful pattern into your lifelong obligation.

Your commitment to staying is real. You don’t have to prove it by promising to make repair your responsibility alone.

Tell the plate-maker: “Please hold printing; the wording isn’t final.”

so what now. i tell him i can't say it because it sounds too one-sided. or i print the truth.

because that's what this is. the truth.

I believe you that it’s the truth. And I was too categorical about what you should do with it.

**You don’t have to choose between hiding the truth and promising it will always be this way.** “This is what our relationship has been” and “this is what I vow to keep doing” are different statements. Your words do both.

You don’t need to tell Mateo, “I can’t say this because it sounds one-sided.” You could tell him:

> “I wrote these because they’re true to my experience. I love you, and I want to stay when things are hard. But reading them back, I need to know: when we lose each other, will you take responsibility for coming back toward me, too? I’m willing to swallow my pride. I need that willingness from you as well.”

I can’t know his intentions or your whole marriage from these lines. But three days of silence—and your expectation that you’ll always be the one to end it—deserve attention beyond the wording on a plate.

You can hold the printing without retracting your love or denying your experience. **The truth deserves to be spoken. It doesn’t have to become a vow tonight.**
